sessions.task: Fix her four-year-old phone whose battery dies mid-morning before her first day of the fall term, and ask for settings that stretch it through a long day.

turns.text: ok my phone is dying every morning and its the first day of term.. its a 4 year old phone w a cracked corner and the battery drops like crazy, was at 40% by 7 this morning even tho i charged it overnight 🫠

That's rough on a first day. A battery that drops that fast is usually aging plus something draining it in the background. Quick fixes to try now:

- Turn on Low Power / Battery Saver mode
- Lower screen brightness and set auto-lock to 30 seconds
- Check Settings > Battery and see which apps use the most; force-close or restrict the worst ones
- Turn off Background App Refresh for apps you don't need live
- Switch off Bluetooth, and Location for apps that don't need it
- Use dark mode if your screen is OLED

What kind of phone is it (iPhone or Android)? I can give exact menu steps.
iphone. also i need it to last til like 6pm, im at the cafe noon to 6 today so it has to survive class AND the shift

Got it. For iPhone, noon to 6 at the cafe plus class means you need roughly 12+ hours. Steps:

- Settings > Battery > turn on Low Power Mode (or add it to Control Center)
- Settings > Battery > check Battery Health. If max capacity is under ~80%, a battery replacement at Apple or a repair shop will fix the root problem
- Settings > General > Background App Refresh > Off (or Wi-Fi only)
- Settings > Display & Brightness > Auto-Lock > 30 Seconds, Auto-Brightness on
- Settings > Privacy > Location Services > set most apps to While Using or Never
- Settings > Mail > Fetch New Data > Manual or hourly
- Turn off Raise to Wake

Also carry a small power bank or keep a charger at the cafe so you can top up during the shift.
ok that helps. one more thing, can i set calendar reminders to replace my paper planner? i normally use a paper planner w washi tape and plan the week on sunday nights but i cant carry it around rn

Sure, and it's lighter on battery than you'd think. Setup:

- Open Calendar > tap + to add an event > set the time and choose an Alert (e.g. 30 minutes before)
- Make separate calendars for classes, work and personal (Calendars > Add Calendar) and give each a color, like your washi tape
- Use Repeat > Every Week for recurring classes and shifts
- Do a Sunday night weekly setup: add everything for the week in one sitting, just like your planner
- Turn on Siri suggestions off if you want less background use

Calendar alerts are local notifications, so they barely drain the battery. Want me to turn your week into a list you can type in?
yes pls but later, ty!! ok im gonna go charge it ☕
Sounds good! Plug in a charger or power bank when you can, and good luck on your first day. Come back whenever you want that week list made.

sessions.task: Ask how to memorize muscle origins and insertions quickly, after anatomy class that morning where classmates were already talking about the practical.

turns.text: ok wait random but how do i memorize muscle origins and insertions fast.. everyone in anatomy was already talking about the practical today and i feel behind 🫠

You're not behind, and origins and insertions are very learnable with a system. Here's a quick way in:

- **Learn by region, not alphabetically.** Do one group at a time (for example the rotator cuff) so the muscles share landmarks.
- **Name the bones first.** Origin is usually the more fixed, proximal attachment and insertion the more mobile, distal one. If you know the bones, half the work is done.
- **Make a story with the action.** Contraction pulls the insertion toward the origin, so you can predict the movement from the attachments.
- **Draw it.** Sketch the bone and add the muscle as a line from origin to insertion.
- **Say it aloud, then self-test.** Cover the answer and recite origin, insertion, action, nerve.

Do you take notes in any particular system? I can tailor the tips.
yes i do color coded, pink for muscles so thats where all this goes. can u make the tips match that

Sure, here's a version that fits your pink-for-muscles system:

- **Pink = the muscle.** Write the muscle name and action in pink.
- **Blue = its bones.** Underline the origin and insertion landmarks in blue, since those are bone features. The pink and blue then sit side by side.
- **Green = nerve.** Add the innervation in green so each muscle links to a nerve.
- **Yellow = likely test items.** Highlight in yellow only what your instructor stressed or is likely to be tested.
- **One muscle per line:** pink name → blue origin → blue insertion → action → green nerve.

That gives you one consistent row per muscle that you can scan quickly.
ooh nice. also how do i turn it into flashcards for my deck. i review on breaks so they need to be quick

Good use of break time. Keep cards small and one-directional:

- **Front:** muscle name. **Back:** origin, insertion, action, nerve in four short lines.
- **Reverse cards:** front "What attaches to the [bone landmark]?" and back the muscle. These help with identifying muscles from a model or specimen.
- **Action cards:** front "Which muscle does [movement]?" and back the answer and nerve.
- **Keep it to one fact cluster per card**, and split anything long into two cards.
- **Add a tiny image** if your app allows, such as a labeled diagram.
- **Add 10 to 15 new cards a day** rather than a big batch, so reviews stay manageable.

The back should be readable in under five seconds.

Happy to help! Here's a simple setup:

**Sheet 1: Ingredients**
- Columns: Ingredient | Package size | Package price | Unit (g, oz, each) | Cost per unit
- Cost per unit = price ÷ size

**Sheet 2: Recipe**
- Columns: Ingredient | Amount used per batch | Cost per unit | Line cost
- Line cost = amount × cost per unit
- Add wrappers, oil for frying, and packaging as rows too

**Sheet 3: Per-roll summary**
- Total batch cost = sum of line costs
- Rolls per batch
- Cost per roll = batch cost ÷ rolls per batch
- Optional: waste % (add 5-10% to the batch cost)

- Per-ingredient total = (amount used in g ÷ 100) × value per 100 g
- Sum each column for the whole batch
- Divide by 60 for per-roll numbers
- Frying: don't count all the oil. Weigh the oil before and after and count only what the rolls absorbed
- Sodium usually comes mostly from soy sauce, salt, and the wrappers, so check those labels carefully

Quick answer: homemade cold brew concentrate usually keeps about 7 to 10 days in the fridge in a sealed glass jar or bottle. Some people push to 2 weeks, but the flavor gets flat and a bit woody after the first week.

A few tips:
- Strain it well (fine filter) so grounds don't keep extracting
- Keep it airtight and cold, at the back of the fridge
- Diluted cold brew is best within 3 to 5 days

- Cold brew steeps 12 to 18 hours, and the low temperature gives lower perceived acidity
- Concentrate is usually 1:4 to 1:8 coffee to water, so it's diluted before serving
- Cold-brewed coffee can taste smoother, but it isn't necessarily lower in caffeine
also do u have serving notes for oat milk w it? like ratios. i hate when milk gets over-steamed and tastes burnt so id rather keep it cold or barely warm

Here are bullets:

**Iced (best bet)**
- 1 part concentrate : 1 to 1.5 parts water, over ice
- Add oat milk last, about 2 to 3 oz, and stir gently
- Barista-style oat milk blends in best and doesn't separate

**Barely warm**
- Heat oat milk only to about 130 to 140°F (warm, not hot)
- Anything past 150°F can taste scorched and flat
- Pour it into the diluted cold brew for a mellow hot-ish drink

**Tip**
- Shake oat milk before pouring since it settles
- Don't add oat milk to very acidic coffee that's sat out, since it can curdle

sessions.task: Ask for an explanation of how the sliding filament model of muscle contraction works, before her anatomy lecture.

turns.text: ok wait can u explain the sliding filament model pls. i have anatomy at 9 and im reviewing before lol

Sure! Quick version first: muscles contract when thin filaments (actin) slide past thick filaments (myosin) inside each sarcomere. The filaments don't shorten, they overlap more. Want me to go step by step, or keep it to bullets?
bullets pls, ones i can copy into my notes. muscles are pink in my notes so like make it a pink section ☕

Here you go, a pink section for your notes:

🩷 **Sliding Filament Model**

- **Signal:** a motor neuron releases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, which triggers an action potential in the muscle fiber.
- **Calcium release:** the action potential travels down the T-tubules, and the sarcoplasmic reticulum releases Ca²⁺.
- **Unblocking:** Ca²⁺ binds troponin, which moves tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin.
- **Cross-bridge:** the myosin head (already holding ADP + Pi) binds actin.
- **Power stroke:** myosin pivots, releasing ADP + Pi, and pulls the thin filament toward the center of the sarcomere (the M line).
- **Detach:** a new ATP binds myosin, and the head lets go of actin.
- **Reset:** ATP is hydrolyzed, which re-cocks the myosin head. The cycle repeats as long as Ca²⁺ and ATP are available.
- **Result:** the Z lines move closer, so the sarcomere shortens. The A band stays the same length, while the I band and H zone shrink.
- **Relaxation:** Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the SR, tropomyosin covers the binding sites again, and the muscle relaxes.

Tip: ATP is needed to *release* the myosin head, not to bind it. That's a common exam trap.
omg ok that A band thing is the one i always mix up. i studied alone at the library yesterday and kept getting it wrong 🫠

That's an easy one to mix up. Here's a way to remember it:

- **A band = All stays the same** (the full length of the thick filaments, so it doesn't change)
- **I band = shrinks** (it's only thin filaments, and they get pulled into the overlap)
- **H zone = shrinks** (the gap with only thick filaments disappears as thin ones slide in)

If you want, I can write a few practice questions on this so you can test yourself before class.
yes pls but like 3 max, short. i have like 15 min before i need to leave

1. During contraction, which band stays the same length: A band or I band?
2. What does Ca²⁺ bind to, and what does that cause?
3. What does ATP do in the cross-bridge cycle: bind actin or release myosin from it?

Answers:
1. A band
2. Troponin, which moves tropomyosin off the binding sites on actin
3. Releases myosin from actin

sessions.task: Look up what sodium and fat typically are in fried lumpia and whether baking changes it.

turns.text: hi! quick q.. whats the typical sodium and fat in a fried lumpia (pork one, small cocktail size). and does baking them change it much

Rough numbers for a small fried pork lumpia (about 20-25 g each):

- Calories: ~60-80
- Total fat: ~4-6 g (about 1-2 g saturated)
- Sodium: ~90-160 mg, depending on the filling seasoning and dipping sauce (not included)

Baking vs frying:
- Baked (brushed or sprayed lightly with oil): fat drops roughly 25-40%, so ~2.5-4 g per roll
- Sodium barely changes, since it comes from the filling (soy sauce, salt, seasoning), not the oil
- Texture is a bit less blistered, but still crisp

- Weigh the whole batch of filling and wrappers raw, then count finished rolls to get grams per roll
- Add up fat and sodium for each ingredient (pork, shrimp, soy sauce, salt, wrappers) from package labels or USDA data
- Divide by number of rolls for the per-roll totals
- Add oil absorbed in frying: usually ~1-2 g fat per small roll, which you can estimate by weighing the oil before and after
- Sodium: don't forget soy sauce and any bouillon, they usually dominate

Approximate breakdown per small fried roll (estimates; swap in your recipe's real amounts):

| Component | Fat (g) | Sat fat (g) | Sodium (mg) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ground pork filling (~12 g) | 2.0-2.5 | 0.8-1.0 | 20-30 |

So 5.2 g fat and 138 mg sodium sit inside the range. Frying oil is mostly unsaturated if you use a vegetable oil, so the saturated fat mostly comes from the pork.

sessions.task: Fix her slow, dying phone battery late at night so it can last through a closing shift and an early class.

turns.text: ok Doc needs help, my phone is dying 🫠 its a 4 yr old phone w a cracked corner and the battery drops like 20% in an hour

Happy to help. Four years in, batteries lose a lot of capacity, so let's find the drains first.

Two quick questions:
- iPhone or Android?
- What do you mostly use it for during the day?
android. i have a 600 card flashcard app i go thru on breaks at work and its eating the battery. also i stream a lo-fi playlist while i study

Those two are likely the biggest drains. Here's a fix list, in order:

**Tonight (2 min)**
- Settings > Battery > check usage per app. Confirm the flashcard app and music app are top.
- Turn on Battery Saver / Adaptive Battery.
- Set screen timeout to 30 sec and drop brightness, or turn on auto-brightness.
- Turn off background refresh and location for apps you don't need.

**Flashcards**
- Use dark mode in the app if it has one (big savings on OLED screens).
- Turn off sync/animations if there's an option.
- Download the deck for offline use so it isn't pinging the network.

**Music**
- Download the playlist instead of streaming.
- Lower the audio quality setting.
- Use wired earbuds if you have them; Bluetooth adds a bit more drain.

**Hardware reality check**
A cracked corner and fast drops can mean a worn battery. A replacement at a phone repair shop is usually cheap and can fix it for good. If the phone gets warm or the battery looks swollen, stop using it and get it checked.

- **Now:** do the settings above, then plug in and charge to 100%. Use the original charger if you can.
- **6:45 a.m.:** unplug. Keep Battery Saver on all day.
- **Class:** airplane mode or silent, screen off.
- **Breaks at work:** use the flashcards offline and keep sessions short, 5-10 min.
- **Music:** downloaded only, one earbud if you can.
- **Backup:** bring a small power bank or a charger and a cable. Many cafes have an outlet near the counter, so ask if you can plug in during a slow stretch.

If you want an extra buffer, charge for a few minutes whenever you're sitting down anywhere, even 10-15% helps.

sessions.task: Look up what to check when buying a used e-bike, such as battery health and range, before seeing one on Saturday.

turns.text:

Good plan, and sorry about the stolen bike. The battery is the most expensive part, so start there. Here's a rundown:

**Battery and range**
- Ask the seller for the battery's age and how many charge cycles it has had. Most last about 500-1,000 cycles.
- Ask for the real-world range on one charge, then compare it to the manufacturer's claim. A big gap means a worn battery.
- Look for swelling, cracks, rust on the contacts, or a case that has been opened.
- Make sure it charges. Ask them to show it charging, and check that the charger fits and isn't a knockoff.
- On the display, check that the battery bars drop gradually. Fast drops under load mean weak cells.

**Motor and ride**
- Test ride for at least 10-15 minutes, including a hill if you can.
- Listen for grinding or clicking. Check that the assist engages smoothly with no jerking.
- Try every assist level.

**Frame and parts**
- Look for cracks near the welds and the battery mount.
- Check the brakes, tire wear, chain wear and wobble in the wheels.
- Spin the pedals and check the gears shift cleanly.

**Paperwork**
- Get the brand and model so you can look up the original price.
- Ask for the receipt or proof of ownership. Since yours was stolen, you really don't want to buy a stolen bike.
- Ask about warranty transfer, if there is one.

Want me to turn this into a shorter checklist you can run through on the spot?
yes pls!! too long lol. just bullets i can go thru in order at the seller's place

Here's the short version, in the order to do it:

**Before the ride (5 min)**

- [ ] Ask: battery age and charge cycles?
- [ ] Ask: real range on one charge?
- [ ] Receipt or proof of ownership
- [ ] Brand and model (look up the price later)

**Test ride (10-15 min)**
- [ ] Battery charge level at start, then again at the end. How much did it drop?
- [ ] Try every assist level
- [ ] Assist engages smoothly
- [ ] No grinding or clicking from the motor
- [ ] Brakes grab evenly
- [ ] Gears shift cleanly
- [ ] Ride a hill if one is nearby

**After the ride (5 min)**
- [ ] Plug it in and confirm it charges
- [ ] Check wheels for wobble and tires for wear
- [ ] Check the frame for cracks near welds
- [ ] Take photos of the serial number

If anything fails, use it to negotiate the price down or walk away. Good luck on Saturday!

Happy to help! The 12 cranial nerves are traditionally numbered with Roman numerals, and each one is classified as sensory (S), motor (M), or both (B). Here they are in order, along with their main functions. Since the standard mnemonic is off the table, one good approach is to group them by region and function, then build a story or image for each group. For instance, the first two nerves are purely sensory and deal with smell and vision, the next three control eye movement, and so on. After that, I'd suggest quizzing yourself in both directions: number to name and function to number. Spaced repetition in your flashcard app would help too. Would you like me to walk through each nerve in detail, along with example exam questions and common clinical tests?
too long just bullets pls

Here you go, in green 🟩 (I can't change text color, so I've marked each line with a green square to match your notes):

🟩 I Olfactory – smell (S)
🟩 II Optic – vision (S)
🟩 III Oculomotor – most eye movements, eyelid lift, pupil constriction (M)
🟩 IV Trochlear – eye movement, superior oblique (M)
🟩 V Trigeminal – face sensation, chewing muscles (B)
🟩 VI Abducens – eye moves outward (M)
🟩 VII Facial – facial expression, taste front 2/3 of tongue (B)
🟩 VIII Vestibulocochlear – hearing, balance (S)
🟩 IX Glossopharyngeal – taste back of tongue, swallowing (B)
🟩 X Vagus – heart, gut, voice box (B)
🟩 XI Accessory – shoulder shrug, head turn (M)
🟩 XII Hypoglossal – tongue movement (M)

Fastest memory tricks:
- Chunk them: I-II senses, III-IV-VI eyes, V-VII face, VIII-IX-X-XI-XII the rest
- Eye trick: LR6 SO4, everything else is III (lateral rectus = VI, superior oblique = IV)

All correct! Absorption, beyond the unit:

Fun plan! A skeleton face is the easiest version to keep clean. Here's a simple approach:

- Base: pour a full cup of latte with a flat, even white canvas of microfoam. Skip any rosetta or heart; you want a blank surface.
- Dark layer: pour the white foam as a solid circle, and leave a thin brown crema ring around the edge.
- Etching: use a toothpick or etching pen dipped in the dark crema or a little chocolate sauce.
  - Eyes: two oval sockets, filled in
  - Nose: small upside-down heart or triangle
  - Mouth: a straight line with short vertical teeth lines
- Tip: wipe the tool between each feature so the lines stay sharp.

Nice, a steady pour is exactly what fine etching needs. Timing:

- Pour: about 8-10 seconds total. Start high and thin to build the crema, then lower the pitcher and push the foam in to make a solid white circle.
- Foam: slightly less stretched than for a rosetta. Tight, glossy microfoam with no big bubbles holds longest.
- Etch right away: you have roughly 30-60 seconds before the foam starts to separate and lines blur.
- Rush strategy: pour several cups, then etch them in a batch only if they sit under a minute. Otherwise do one at a time. Keep sauce pre-loaded in a small squeeze bottle so you aren't hunting for it.
- Serve fast: the drink is best handed over within a couple of minutes.

Sure! Here's the path food takes, with the main enzymes:

- **Mouth**: chewing + salivary amylase (starch to smaller sugars), lingual lipase
- **Pharynx → esophagus**: swallowing, peristalsis (no digestion)
- **Stomach**: pepsin (proteins), HCl activates it, gastric lipase (a little fat)
- **Small intestine**: duodenum, jejunum, ileum. Most digestion and absorption happens here
- **Large intestine**: water absorption, gut bacteria, forms feces
- **Rectum → anus**: elimination

Accessory organs: salivary glands, liver (bile), gallbladder (stores bile), pancreas (amylase, lipase, proteases, bicarbonate).

Happy to help. Let's start with a quick check of the core method, then you can try a problem.

**Stoichiometry in 4 steps**
- Balance the equation
- Grams to moles (divide by molar mass)
- Moles to moles (use the coefficient ratio)
- Moles to grams (multiply by molar mass)

**Try this one:** How many grams of H2O form when 8.0 g of H2 reacts with excess O2?
2H2 + O2 → 2H2O

What do you get for step 2 (moles of H2)? Show me whatever you've got, even if it's rough.

Yes, 3.96 mol H2.

- Ratio H2:H2O is 2:2, so 1:1 → 3.96 mol H2O
- Molar mass H2O = 18.02 g/mol
- 3.96 × 18.02 ≈ **71 g H2O**

Next type is limiting reactant:
- Convert each reactant to moles
- Divide each by its coefficient
- Smaller number = limiting
- Use the limiting one for the answer

sessions.task: Look up how to dry out a cold-weather commute soaked in the first storm and what to do about a mild cold, plus whether e-bike electronics are safe to ride in heavy rain.

turns.text: ok so i got caught in the storm today and im kind of a drowned rat 🫠 biked to gen chem at 11 in the downpour and showed up soaked. how do i dry out my stuff and not get sick, i think im already getting a cold

Ugh, sorry. Here's a quick plan.

**Drying out your stuff**
- Take out the insides of your shoes and stuff them with crumpled newspaper or paper towels. Swap them when damp.
- Dry your bag open, upside down, away from direct heat.
- Hang wet clothes on a rack with airflow. A fan helps more than a heater.
- Put damp books or notes between towels and press gently. Avoid hairdryers on paper.

**For you**
- Warm shower, dry clothes, warm drink.
- Rain doesn't cause colds, but being chilled can make you feel worse.

What symptoms do you have?
scratchy throat and stuffy nose, nothing crazy. i want stuff that actually works but i go to bed around 12:30 and im up at 6:45 so nothing that knocks me out or keeps me up pls

Got it, mild symptoms and a short sleep window:

- **Throat:** warm tea with honey, salt-water gargle, lozenges
- **Stuffy nose:** saline spray or a steamy shower before bed; a second pillow helps drainage
- **Fluids:** water all evening
- **Avoid:** anything labeled "PM" or with diphenhydramine (drowsy), and decongestants close to bedtime since they can keep you awake
- **Sleep:** aim for 7 hours if you can; rest does more than any pill

If you get a fever, trouble breathing, or it lasts over about 10 days, check in with a doctor.
ok good. also my phone is super old, like 4 yrs, cracked corner and the battery is bad, and it nearly died in the rain. any cheap waterproof pouch options

Yes, a few cheap options:

- **Universal waterproof pouch (about $5-12):** Look for an IPX8 rating and a double-lock seal. You can still use the touchscreen through it.
- **Zip-top freezer bag:** Free backup. Works, but the screen is fiddly.
- **Handlebar or bike phone mount with a rain cover:** Handy if you ride a lot.
- **Inside pocket of your bag, wrapped in a bag:** Keeps it out of the downpour.

A cracked corner can let water in, so a pouch is smart. If it got wet, power it off and let it dry for a day. Don't charge it while damp. Skip the rice trick.
thanks. last thing, its a used ebike i got for $640 and i charge it behind the cafe counter. is it ok that i rode it thru the storm?? are the electronics safe in heavy rain

Most e-bikes handle ordinary rain fine, since the battery, motor, and controller are designed to be splash-resistant. Heavy rain and puddles are different, and a used bike's seals may have worn.

**Do now**
- Wipe the bike down with a towel, especially around the battery, display, and connectors.
- Store it indoors somewhere dry.
- Let it dry fully before charging, ideally a few hours, so the battery contacts aren't wet.
- Check the battery contacts and charging port for water.

**Watch for**
- Display flickering, cutting out, error codes, or odd noises
- A battery that's unusually hot or smells odd. Stop using it and get it checked.

**Going forward**
- Don't ride through deep puddles above the hub or pedals.
- Don't pressure-wash it.
- Ask the seller or a bike shop about its water rating.

Charging it behind the counter is fine as long as it's dry first and sits on a hard surface away from anything flammable.
ok ill let it dry before i charge it. thank u!! ok im gonna go shower now
Sounds good. Warm shower, dry clothes, tea with honey. Feel better soon! ☕

sessions.task: Tutoring: explain how to balance chemical equations and check a stoichiometry problem set before Thursday's chem class.

turns.text:
ok can u explain how to balance chemical equations pls

im in general chem tue/thu at 11 and i wanna finish this problem set ahead of it. kenji drives me so i usually study in the library after, but its late and i need it to make sense now

Sure. Here's the short version:

**Balancing steps**
1. Write the unbalanced equation with correct formulas.
2. Count each element's atoms on both sides.
3. Change only coefficients (the big numbers in front), never subscripts.
4. Balance elements that appear in one compound per side first. Save O and H for last, and treat polyatomic ions like (SO4) as one unit if they appear unchanged on both sides.
5. If you get a fraction, multiply everything by the denominator.
6. Recount every element.

**Example:** C3H8 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O
- C: 3 on the left, so CO2 gets a 3
- H: 8 on the left, so H2O gets a 4
- O: 6 + 4 = 10 on the right, so O2 gets a 5
- Result: C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O

**Stoichiometry afterward:**
grams -> moles (molar mass) -> mole ratio (from coefficients) -> moles of the other substance -> grams

Want to send a problem from your set and I'll check your work?

ok wait that makes sense. here's one i did

N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3. how many grams NH3 from 10.0 g H2?

my work: 10.0 g / 2.02 = 4.95 mol H2. times 2/3 = 3.30 mol NH3. times 17.03 = 56.2 g

Your setup is right, and so is the mole ratio (2 NH3 per 3 H2).

Checking the numbers:
- 10.0 g / 2.02 g/mol = 4.95 mol H2 ✓
- 4.95 x 2/3 = 3.30 mol NH3 ✓
- 3.30 x 17.03 g/mol = 56.2 g NH3 ✓

Sig figs: your starting value has 3, so 56.2 g is correct.

One extra check: the answer should be bigger than 10 g, because N atoms are being added to the H. It is, so it passes.

Send the next one if you want it checked.
nice. theres a harder one w a limiting reactant, ill send a pic of my worked page

Sounds good. A photo of the page works, and if the handwriting is hard to read you can also type out the numbers. I'll check the balanced equation, the mole conversions, and which reactant you picked as limiting.

ugh my phone died halfway thru taking the pic, its old and the battery is awful 🫠 ok typing it instead

2Al + 3Cl2 -> 2AlCl3. 5.00 g Al and 8.00 g Cl2. i got Al = 0.185 mol, Cl2 = 0.113 mol. said Cl2 is limiting bc its smaller

Good instinct to check, but you can't pick the limiting reactant just by comparing mole amounts. You have to account for the ratio.

**Your mole values are right:**
- 5.00 / 26.98 = 0.185 mol Al ✓
- 8.00 / 70.90 = 0.113 mol Cl2 ✓

**Compare using the ratio (2 Al : 3 Cl2):**
- 0.185 mol Al needs 0.185 x 3/2 = 0.278 mol Cl2. You only have 0.113, so Cl2 runs out first.

So Cl2 is limiting, and your conclusion is correct, but the reasoning matters. Here it worked because Cl2 has fewer moles AND needs a bigger share per Al. Always use the ratio check.

**Product:**
0.113 mol Cl2 x 2/3 = 0.0753 mol AlCl3
0.0753 x 133.34 g/mol = 10.0 g AlCl3

Want this as a bulleted checklist you can paste into your notes?
yes pls, color tagged to match my notes, yellow for stuff thatll be on the test lol

**Limiting reactant checklist**

🟦 **Setup**
- Balance the equation, then recount every element
- Convert each given mass to moles

🟩 **Find the limiting reactant**
- Pick one reactant and calculate the moles of the other it would need, using the coefficients
- If you don't have enough of the other one, that one is limiting

🟨 **Likely on the test**
- Use the ratio, not just "smaller number of moles"
- Do product calculations from the limiting reactant only
- Convert moles of product to grams using molar mass
- Match sig figs to your given data

🟪 **Final check**
- Is the product mass plausible, and under the total mass of the reactants?

Good luck with the problem set! Get some rest.

sessions.task: Look up what a registered dietitian does and the Bayshore State path, including prerequisites she'd need.

turns.text: hi! can u explain what a registered dietitian actually does day to day? and what the path looks like at bayshore state, prereqs too pls

Sure! Here's an overview.

**What an RD does**
- Assesses nutrition needs and builds meal or care plans
- Works in hospitals, clinics, schools, food companies, sports and public health programs
- Medical nutrition therapy: diabetes, kidney disease, heart disease, digestive issues
- Counseling, education, and charting

**Typical US path**
- Bachelor's or master's from an accredited (ACEND) program
- Supervised practice internship, roughly 1,000 hours
- National registration exam
- State licensure where required

**Prereqs (common)**
- General chemistry, organic chemistry, biochemistry
- Anatomy & physiology, microbiology
- Intro nutrition, statistics
- Psychology or sociology

I don't have Bayshore State's current catalog, so check their nutrition or dietetics page for the exact requirements. Which classes have you already taken? I can map what's left.
ok wait. im taking anatomy and gen chem 1 rn, stats online. planning intro to nutrition in spring

That's a solid start. Based on the typical list:

**Done or in progress**
- Anatomy & Physiology I (then II)
- General Chem I (then II)
- Statistics

**Likely still needed**
- Anatomy & Physiology II
- General Chem II, then organic chem and biochem
- Microbiology
- Intro to Nutrition (spring, as planned)
- Psychology or sociology

**Next steps**
1. Pull Bayshore's dietetics requirements sheet
2. Compare it with your community college's course equivalencies (assist.org-style articulation, if your state has it)
3. Ask your transfer counselor which courses are priority before you apply

Got it. Here's a rough plan in bullets, assuming a few terms before transfer:

**Spring**
- Intro to Nutrition
- A&P II
- General Chem II

**Summer or fall (before transfer)**
- Microbiology
- Psychology or sociology
- Organic chem if offered, otherwise at the university

**Transfer year**
- Biochem, food science, nutrition courses in the major
- Apply for supervised practice near the end

**Good news for flexibility**
- Anatomy, chem and stats count toward nutrition and public health, and also nursing or pharmacy, so nothing you're taking now is wasted.

That last bit may help with a conversation at home. Want help with that too?
yeah. the pharmacy talk is still not happening.. how do i prepare for it

Here's a simple way to prepare:

- **Pick one goal**: just share that you're exploring nutrition and public health, not announce a final decision
- **Lead with something concrete**: what the job is, that it uses the same science classes, and that you've mapped a plan
- **Acknowledge their hopes**: say you appreciate what they want for you
- **Choose the moment**: a calm time, not right after a work shift
- **Have a first line ready**: "I've been looking into something I really like, can I show you?"
- **Bring the plan**: the course list above on one page

It also helps to expect questions like "what about the money?" Dietitians have steady demand, and you can look up current salary data to bring along.

- **Time cap:** 2 short blocks a day, 30–45 min each. Stop when the timer ends.
- **Best slots:**
  - Mon, Wed, Fri: after the 9am anatomy class, or before you leave for the shuttle.
  - Tue, Thu: after chem, once Kenji drops you home.
  - Sat, Sun: about 2:30–3:30, after the cafe and Lotus Nails.

  - Mon: bones (blue)
  - Wed: muscles (pink)
  - Thu: nerves (green)
  - Fri: yellow list
  - Tue: chem
- **Flashcards:** do 50 cards on breaks, and only review the ones you miss.
- **Sunday check:** add the study blocks to your planner with washi tape, with one block a day at most.
- **Off-limits:** no studying after 9pm, and no studying while you eat. Wednesday closing shifts start tomorrow, so Wednesday nights stay free.
- **Rest day:** pick one afternoon with no studying. Saturday works well, since you'll be tired after opening.
- **Weekly check-in:** 5 minutes on Sunday to count your misses and pick the next week's focus.

- **Pick one anchor spot**: a corner of a desk, a dining table end, or a shelf-and-chair nook. Same spot every time so your brain switches into "study mode" quickly.
- **Use a "study kit" box or tray**: laptop, notebooks, pens, charger, headphones all live in one container. Study = grab the box. Done = box goes back on a shelf or in a closet.
- **Go vertical, not wide**: a small shelf, wall organizer, or pegboard for reference materials instead of spreading things across surfaces.
- **Fold-away options**: a laptop stand plus a lap desk or a wall-mounted fold-down desk if floor space is tight.
- **Set a visual boundary**: a small lamp or a desk mat that signals "on." Turn it off or roll it up when you're done.
- **Keep digital stuff tidy too**: one folder for everything, a single notes app, bookmarks bar for key links, so there's no paper pile growing.
- **Lighting and comfort basics**: a decent task lamp, a chair that doesn't wreck your back, and a cushion or footrest if needed. These matter more than extra gear.
- **Time-box it**: pick set study windows (e.g., 2 blocks a day) so the setup only "exists" during those times.
- **Noise plan**: noise-cancelling headphones or a low-fi/white noise playlist if the space is shared.
- **End-of-session reset (2 min)**: clear the surface, jot tomorrow's first task on a sticky note, and pack the kit away.
- **Weekly mini-purge**: recycle old printouts and scrap notes so clutter doesn't accumulate.

Short answer: it depends on your field, but "already" is often not too early, and it's rarely only a 3rd-year thing.

**Why October can matter:**
- In competitive, structured fields (finance, consulting, big tech, some engineering and big-company programs), applications for next summer often open in the fall and sometimes close by November or December. Those can fill early.
- In most other fields (smaller companies, startups, research, nonprofits, government, many co-ops), hiring runs from roughly January to April, so you have time.

**If you're in 1st or 2nd year:**
- Many large companies run early-career or "discovery" programs aimed at first- and second-years, and they're less competitive than the standard internship pipeline.
- Realistic goals for now: get a resume together, get it reviewed by your career center, and apply to a few programs that are open to your year. Don't expect to land your dream role.

For a direct deposit form, you'll typically need:

- **Bank name**
- **Account type**: checking or savings
- **Routing number**: 9 digits (ABA number)
- **Account number**
- **Name on the account**, as it appears at the bank

You may also need to provide:
- **Your signature and the date**, since the form is an authorization
- **A voided check** or a bank letter/statement, which some employers require to verify the account
- **Split deposit details**, if you want part of your pay going to a second account (amount or percentage for each)
- **Your employee ID**, if the form asks for it

**Where to find the numbers:**
- On a check, the routing number is the first set of digits at the bottom left, and the account number is the second set.
- Your bank's app or website usually lists both under account details. Use the ACH or direct deposit routing number, since it can differ from the wire routing number at some banks.

Double-check every digit before you hand it over. A single wrong number can delay your first deposit. It's also worth asking Beatrice when the change takes effect, since you may get one more paper check before it kicks in.
